Forensics

Four published accounting-quality screens. Each carries its formula and its paper, hover any score.

Beneish M-2.64ComputationEight-ratio earnings-manipulation score. Below −1.78 is the non-manipulator range.M = −4.84 + 0.92·DSRI + 0.528·GMI + 0.404·AQI + 0.892·SGI + 0.115·DEPI − 0.172·SGAI + 4.679·TATA − 0.327·LVGIBeneish (1999) · engine/compute/forensics.py
Altman Z8.93ComputationBankruptcy-risk score. Above 2.99 is the safe zone; below 1.81 distress.Z = 1.2·A + 1.4·B + 3.3·C + 0.6·D + 1.0·EAltman (1968) · engine/compute/forensics.py
Piotroski F6ComputationNine binary tests of profitability, leverage and efficiency. 8–9 is strong.F = Σ of nine signals (profitability 4, leverage/liquidity 3, efficiency 2)Piotroski (2000) · engine/compute/forensics.py
Sloan accrual-0.05ComputationAccrual share of earnings. High accruals predict lower future returns.Accruals = (net income − cash flow from operations) / average total assetsSloan (1996) · engine/compute/forensics.py

The comparable-company view leans on the fiscal-year, 7 peers basis. both bases have 7 usable peers; fiscal year is preferred on a tie because every peer files an annual report, while a trailing table drops whoever does not report quarters. Every multiple below carries the basis and the peer count it was formed from, because a median over two peers and one over seven are different claims rather than a weaker and a stronger version of the same one.

Audit trail

What the verifier checked and what it deleted. Prompt §39 asks for rejected claims to be published rather than quietly dropped, so a reader can judge the deletion as well as the claim.

No verification record
This page was rendered without a verifier report, engine report on a saved run rebuilds the page but not the verification, which happens as each phase completes.

Ensemble, council and bias checks

Disagreement map

One run only
Prompt §39 asks where the council seats and the retained runs disagreed most, and how it was resolved. This page was rendered from one run, and a single run has no disagreement to map and no dispersion to report. Build an ensemble with engine ensemble TICKER.

Bias checks

One run only
SPEC §10's blinded and order-effect checks compare a run against the ensemble's retained answer, so they run once per ensemble rather than once per run.

Glossary

Every term this report uses, in plain English, with what it does not tell you (§39).

Accrual ratio
Earnings not backed by cash, as a share of assets. Persistently high accruals are the most-studied warning sign in accounting research (Sloan 1996).
ADV
Average daily volume. How much of the stock trades in a normal day, which bounds how large a position can be entered or exited.
Altman Z
A bankruptcy-risk score from five balance-sheet ratios (Altman 1968). Above about 3 is the safe zone for a manufacturer.
Alpha
Return not explained by the market or by the factor model being used. It is defined relative to a model, so it changes when the model does.
Beneish M
An earnings-manipulation score from eight accounting ratios (Beneish 1999). Above -1.78 is the flag, which is a screen and not a verdict.
Beta
How much the stock has moved for a one-percent move in the benchmark. Measured over a window, so it is a description of the past.
Blume adjustment
Shrinking a measured beta toward one, because high and low betas both drift back over time (Blume 1971).
Comps
Comparable-company analysis: valuing a company at the multiples its peers trade on, which answers “what is this worth to the market”, not “what is this worth”.
Days to cover
Short interest divided by average daily volume: how many days of normal trading it would take the shorts to buy back their position.
DCF
Discounted cash flow. The value of a business as the cash it will produce, discounted for time and risk. Its answer is only as good as its drivers.
Distance to default
How many standard deviations of asset value separate a company from the point where its assets equal its debts (Merton 1974).
DuPont decomposition
Splitting return on equity into margin, asset turnover and leverage, so a rising return can be read as efficiency or as borrowing.
EPV
Earnings power value: the business valued on current earnings with no growth. A floor that does not depend on a forecast (Greenwald).
EV
Enterprise value: the value of the whole business, debt included, before subtracting what the lenders own.
Factor exposure
How much of a return is explained by known drivers - size, value, profitability, momentum - rather than by the company itself (Fama and French).
FCF
Free cash flow: cash from operations less the capital spending needed to keep the business running.
Kelly fraction
The bet size that maximises long-run growth given an edge. A raw Kelly above one says the inputs are too confident, not that leverage is advisable.
LBO ceiling
The most a leveraged buyer could pay and still earn its required return. Another floor under the price, not a forecast.
Market impact
The price move caused by trading itself. Estimated here with a square-root law, which is an approximation and never a quotable cost.
Monte Carlo
Running a valuation thousands of times with drawn inputs, to get a distribution instead of a single number. The distribution inherits the assumptions.
NOPAT
Net operating profit after tax: operating profit as if the company had no debt, which is what a DCF discounts.
Point-in-time
Using only information published on or before the analysis date. Without it a backtest learns from the future and looks brilliant.
Reverse DCF
Solving for the growth or margin the current price implies, which turns “is it cheap” into “what would have to be true”.
ROIC
Return on invested capital. Above the cost of capital, growth creates value; below it, growth destroys value.
Sales-to-capital
How much revenue each unit of invested capital supports, used to turn a growth forecast into a capital-spending forecast (Damodaran).
Sharpe ratio
Return per unit of volatility. It treats upside and downside volatility alike, which flatters strategies that lose rarely and badly.
Short interest
Shares sold short and not yet bought back, reported twice a month by the exchanges with a lag.
Terminal value
The value of everything beyond the forecast window. Where most of a DCF usually sits, which is why its share of the total is checked.
WACC
Weighted average cost of capital: the blended return debt and equity holders require, and the rate a DCF discounts at.
13F
The quarterly holdings report large institutions file 45 days after quarter end. Late, and only institutions.

Disclaimer

This is research output, not investment advice, and nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security. It was produced by an automated engine from free public data as of the analysis date above.

Model limitations worth holding in mind. Every forward number is a projection from a model whose drivers are stated and arguable, not a forecast. The scores are uncalibrated until the backtest in M7, so an 80 does not yet mean anything empirical. The data is free data: no consensus estimates, no options chain, no transcripts, no market-size research, no borrow costs, and 13F holdings are 45 days stale. Everything the engine could not get is listed under “what we did not analyze” rather than estimated.

Charts that could not be drawn, 35

chart
chart 3 (Segment revenue mix): this snapshot has no segment facts: companyfacts serves only undimensioned facts, and the per-filing XBRL loader that reads the segment axis (T6.25) arrived after it was built. A snapshot built from now on will carry them; until then P01 reads the segment footnote with a citation.
chart
chart 8 (Guidance vs actual): no guidance figure in this snapshot could be matched to a metric and a period without guessing. The EX-99 loader (T6.25) reads the press releases; a snapshot built before it exists carries none at all.
chart
chart 9 (Project promise vs delivery): the promise dates come from filing and call text that P03 reads with citations, not from a frame, so there is nothing numeric to plot. P03's promise-versus-delivery table carries the same content as prose.
chart
chart 10 (Competitor benchmark and market share): market share needs a market size, which is sold by market-research firms and is in no free source (the same gap P05 registers). The peer benchmark table carries the comparable part: growth, margin and relative size.
chart
chart 11 (Input-cost sensitivity on gross margin): no bill-of-materials or commodity-exposure data: companyfacts gives cost of revenue as one line, so the elasticity of gross margin to any single input cannot be computed without fabricating the mix.
chart
chart 12 (Macro sensitivities): no macro regression: the snapshot has fewer than a year of aligned weekly observations for the subject and the macro series
chart
chart 13 (Insider dealing over the price): no Form 4 transactions in the snapshot for this issuer
chart
chart 14 (Short interest and days to cover): no short-interest series in the snapshot
chart
chart 15 (Implied volatility term structure and skew): no options chain in this snapshot. The yfinance chain loader (T6.26) fetches one and the daily archiver keeps the history; a snapshot built before they existed carries none, and no free source serves a historical chain.
chart
chart 16 (Estimate revisions and target dispersion): no consensus in this snapshot. These are not licensed data as this chart used to say - the free yfinance aggregate carries a target mean, high and low, and the T6.26 loader fetches it. What is genuinely missing is *history*: the vendor serves only the current reading, so the revision series starts when the daily archiver does.
